description: HealthSheets is a daily crew check-in service that helps spot early signs of astronaut health and wellbeing concerns, without adding admin to astronauts’ workloads. Each day, astronauts complete short morning and evening questionnaires, an hourly timesheet and quick observations about two crewmates. Health teams get the context they need to identify patterns early, while Operations sees only submission status and never health answers.

details:
HealthSheets

HealthSheets adds crew wellbeing data collection to a standard timesheets process through a few short prompts a day, : a morning and evening check-in, two peer observations of assigned crewmates, and an end-of-day timesheet.

Health reviews wellbeing check-ins and peer observations, and Operations reviews timesheets. Each team sees only a status signal for the other’s pending work, so they hold each other accountable without sharing sensitive content. An assistive AI lens helps Health prioritise and spot patterns over time with additional context from undertaken tasks, and gives Operations context such as missed breaks. A human always makes the decision, and AI only provides supporting evidence.

HealthSheets is a monitoring tool, not a clinical records system. Further intervention; like treatment decisions, welfare checks, disciplinaries, and clinical records stay outside the product. Its approach to early identification and contextual monitoring follows NASA OCHMO guidance on behavioral health in spaceflight (OCHMO-TB-016), and it does not replace clinical behavioural-health processes.

Purpose

Audience and why they use HealthSheets:

  • Astronauts: Complete a simple daily check-in without navigating historical sheets or understanding the data model
  • Operations: Track mission activity, working hours, submission completion, and operational follow-up
  • Health: Use questionnaires, peer observations, activity, and trends as contextual evidence for wellbeing monitoring
  • Administrators: Manage system configuration and access

Current implemented state — 15 November 2026

The live app is healthsheets.study (healthsheets.study). Astronaut illustrations are served from cdn.healthsheets.study (cdn.healthsheets.study).

The active demonstration mission is International Space Station (Expedition 75) with seven crew members: Anil Menon (NASA), Pyotr Dubrov (Roscosmos), Anna Kikina (Roscosmos), Jessica Watkins (NASA), Luke Delaney (NASA), Joshua Kutryk (Canadian Space Agency), and Sergey Teteryatnikov (Roscosmos).

All crew and submission data are demonstrations, not real mission or medical records.

Authentication, sign-in and roles

Identity and access use Keycloak, consistent with NASA AppDat core authentication services. Keycloak was chosen because AppDat documents it as its authentication service, integrated with NASA Launchpad for single sign-on and providing OIDC plus centralized user, role, and group management. These capabilities informed the choice; this demonstration deployment is not represented as NASA-operated or formally AppDat-hosted. See the AppDat authentication overview (handbook.appdat.jsc.nasa.gov/docs/core_services/auth) and AppDat Keycloak user guide (handbook.appdat.jsc.nasa.gov/docs/users/keycloak).

Keycloak handles sign-in, session management, and role/group mapping for Astronaut, Operations, Health, and Administrator. Server-side permission checks protect records and actions, including when queued operations are processed. Approvals and privileged actions require a live authenticated session.

Astronauts use /dashboard (also available at /astronaut) and land on their daily dashboard. Operations and Health share Mission Control at /ops; the interface has no separate Health or Admin tab. Accounts with Operations or Health roles can open Mission Control. Accounts with more than one role can use the corresponding views.

Demo accounts

These shared Keycloak accounts are for demonstration use:

  • Anil Menon — anil.menon@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Pyotr Dubrov — pyotr.dubrov@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Anna Kikina — anna.kikina@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Jessica Watkins — jessica.watkins@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Luke Delaney — luke.delaney@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Joshua Kutryk — joshua.kutryk@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Sergey Teteryatnikov — sergey.teteryatnikov@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Astronaut — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Health Professional — health.professional@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Health — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets
  • Operations Officer — operations@nasaspaceapps2026.com — Operations — nasaspaceapps2026-healthsheets

Role permissions

  • Own check-ins, peer observations and timesheet: Astronaut can submit own; Operations and Health have no direct action; Administrator has configuration/access only
  • Crew completion status and history: Astronaut sees own status; Operations and Health see full; Administrator has configuration/access only
  • Pending approval owned by the other team: Operations sees Health-review status only; Health sees timesheet status, content and AI oversight; Administrator has configuration/access only
  • Health questionnaire answers and peer-observation text: Astronaut sees own submissions; Operations has no access; Health has full access; Administrator has no access unless separately assigned Health
  • Timesheets: Astronaut owns own; Operations can view, AI oversight and approval; Health can view as wellbeing context with no approval; Administrator has configuration/access only
  • AI priority and oversight for health submissions: Operations has no access; Health has full access; Administrator has no access unless separately assigned Health
  • Mission configuration: Operations has full; Health has none; Administrator has full
  • Clinical reviews or clinical records: Out of scope for all roles

Administrators manage access and configuration without automatically receiving access to sensitive health records. Health is one department in this version; separate Medical and Behavioural Health role trees are out of scope. Health access to peer observations and activity is not restricted. When operational follow-up is needed, Health contacts Operations outside the platform and does not pass the clinical or questionnaire reason through HealthSheets. Permissions may be refined within a department later.

Current astronaut workflow

The dashboard presents the next outstanding action and today’s requirements: morning check-in, two assigned peer observations, evening check-in and timesheet. It shows due time and Completed, Outstanding, Overdue or Exempt status. A submission is marked complete once saved on the device and syncs in the background. The mission panel is not shown on the astronaut dashboard.

Forms are short guided steps. Wellbeing ratings are 1–5 scales. Low sleep ratings (1–2) prompt a follow-up. “Yes” answers about dangerous behaviour, disputes or something feeling different open a details field. Peer observations refer to the assigned crew member. Timesheets record start and finish times and hourly activities under work, training, break, meal, sleep, interruption or no work.

Astronaut experience

Principle: complete the task and forget about it. Astronauts do not need to understand connectivity, queues, retries, or whether Mission Control has received a submission. They do not browse previous timesheets or health sheets as the primary workflow.

Mission membership and selection

  • An astronaut belongs to one active mission at a time.
  • Training missions count as missions and can establish baselines before an operational mission.
  • Operations manages multiple missions. A mission selector sits above Mission Control so crews and submissions are never mixed across missions.
  • One-mission-at-a-time simplifies membership, questionnaire assignment, peer observation assignment, data attribution, and mission-level reporting.

Home / daily submission cards

Dashboard items for the day (in order):

  • Morning
  • Evening
  • Peer One
  • Peer Two
  • Timesheet

When an item is completed and durably accepted by the application, the card shows completed and the astronaut moves on.

Scoring scale

Consistent 1–5 scale for standard wellbeing questions:

  • 1: Very poor
  • 2: Poor
  • 3: Fair
  • 4: Good
  • 5: Very good

Meaning is question-specific where needed (for example, sleep: 1 = very poor sleep, 5 = very good sleep). Optional explanation of a low score is never forced.

Required responses

Every question requires a response. Free-text fields require an actual written answer. There are no preselected options such as “Nothing to report” or “No additional comments”. The astronaut controls what they disclose.

A partially completed questionnaire may be saved locally if connectivity drops, but it cannot be submitted until all required responses are complete. Free text must meet a minimum meaningful response requirement rather than accepting blanks.



Morning questionnaire

  • How are you feeling physically? — 1–5
  • How are you feeling mentally? — 1–5
  • How well did you sleep? — 1–5
  • How would you rate your energy? — 1–5
  • Is anything bothering you or affecting your ability to work? — Required free text
  • Any additional comments? — Required free text

Evening questionnaire

Captures change during the day without simply repeating the morning check-in. Sleep is not asked again (covered in the morning). Conditional follow-ups keep the form short: free-text detail appears only when the gated answer is yes.

  • How are you feeling physically? — 1–5
  • How are you feeling mentally? — 1–5
  • How would you rate your energy? — 1–5
  • Is anything affecting your ability to work? — Required free text
  • Have you engaged in any dangerous behaviour today? — Yes / No
  • If yes: what happened? — Required free text (shown only if Yes)
  • Have you thought about engaging in dangerous behaviour? — Yes / No
  • If yes: what were you thinking about? — Required free text (shown only if Yes)
  • Have you had any interpersonal disputes today? — Yes / No
  • If yes: what happened? — Required free text (shown only if Yes)
  • Does anything feel different or out of the ordinary? — Yes / No
  • If yes: what feels different? — Required free text (shown only if Yes)
  • Anything else Health should know? — Required free text

Peer observations

Each day the astronaut is prompted to observe two other crew members. Peer observations are completed before the timesheet on the daily dashboard.

  • Have you noticed anything unusual about their behaviour? — Required free text
  • Have they seemed particularly tired, withdrawn, or stressed? — Required free text
  • Have you noticed any positive changes? — Required free text
  • Is there anything you think the Health team should know? — Required free text

Questions stay quick to answer; essays are not required. The same question set is used for Peer One and Peer Two.

Assignment rule

The system automatically assigns two crew members each day, rotating so people are observed by different colleagues over time. Astronauts do not choose who to observe. That reduces social friction and gives Health a broader picture.

Timesheet (end of working day)

Completed at the end of the working day, after peer observations.

  1. Astronaut enters working start and finish times.
  2. HealthSheets generates hourly intervals between those times.
  3. Astronaut records what they did in each interval.
  4. Design accounts for breaks, sleep, interruptions, and periods of no work.
  5. Training activities are recorded against the assigned mission.

Access:

  • Astronauts submit and review their own timesheets.
  • Operations: view, AI oversight and approval for mission activity and accountability.
  • Health: view timesheets as wellbeing context (workload, unusual hours, rest); timesheet approval belongs to Operations.

Health use of data

Health can access:

  • Personal health questionnaires
  • Peer observations
  • Activity and timesheet information
  • Historical submissions and trends
  • Relevant contextual annotations
  • AI prioritisation signals (Health only; asynchronous triage)

Purpose: monitoring and early identification of potential concerns, consistent with the intent of OCHMO-TB-016 Behavioral Health (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-016-behavioral-health.pdf). Not clinical documentation.

HealthSheets shows Operations when a submission is awaiting Health approval, but does not signal that Health wants an operational action or reveal the reason for a separate Health concern; those requests are handled outside the platform.

Current Mission Control and profiles

Mission Control shows illustrated astronaut cards with Morning, Peer 1, Peer 2, Evening and Timesheet status. Each submission has two status lights:

  • Off / Off: Not submitted, or exempt
  • Green / Orange: Submitted and awaiting approval by the responsible team
  • Green / Green: Approved
  • Red / Off: Overdue; Operations can follow up

Health owns approval of check-ins and peer observations. Operations owns timesheet approval. Each team sees a status-only pending-approval signal for submissions assigned to the other team: Operations can see that a Health review is pending, and Health can see that a timesheet awaits Operations approval. The signal provides accountability without giving the other team access to restricted content or controls. Deadlines appear on astronaut profiles.

A dedicated event column sits to the right of the main content and stays available while moving between Mission Control and astronaut profiles. It shows overdue items and new submissions, newest first; pending approvals are shown through the status lights and file cards. Health may see an AI priority label; Operations sees a general submission label. Selecting a submission opens its file in the viewer when the role allows access. Peer-observation events link to the profile of the person observed. Dismissal is stored in the browser. Approval removes that submission from the event feed.

An astronaut profile shows Today’s due times and status lights, a newest-first history timeline, and submission file cards grouped by date. Operations sees timesheets, timesheet AI oversight and operational status; it can approve timesheets. For check-ins and peer observations, Operations sees completion and pending Health approval status only, not answers, AI oversight or approval controls. Health sees all submission content and AI oversight, including timesheets, and can approve check-ins and peer observations. Health sees pending Operations approval on timesheets but cannot approve them. A peer observation appears on both the author’s and subject’s Health profile; it is one submission, and one approval updates its status in both places.

Selecting a file opens a document-style viewer. Only one viewer can be open at a time. The viewer displays submitted answers and, where available, AI oversight. It omits redundant answer chips and the AI model/prompt identifier. Approving updates the corresponding file and lights without reloading the page, then closes the viewer.

Operations - Mission Control

Primary view: mission-wide overview, with individual astronaut Operations profiles opened from it.

Mission selector

Operations switches missions without mixing crew or submission records.

Screen areas

  1. Mission context
    Mission selector, so crews and submissions stay within the selected mission
    Illustrated crew cards and their submission statuses
    A dedicated event column with overdue items and new submissions; pending approvals appear in the status lights and file cards
  2. Crew status
    Illustrated astronaut cards show Morning, Peer 1, Peer 2, Evening and Timesheet status using the two-light matrix. The mission overview is organized around the crew cards and event feed.
  3. Operational attention
    Overdue submissions, shown as red status lights and events for Operations follow-up
    Status-only signal when a check-in or peer observation is awaiting Health approval
    Separate Health requests for operational action remain out of band
  4. Cross-team approval status
    Operations sees which check-ins and peer observations await Health approval, without their contents, AI oversight or approval controls.
    Health sees which timesheets await Operations approval and can view their content and AI oversight, without timesheet approval controls.


Individual Operations profile

Opened when selecting a crew member. Shows mission assignment, submission completion, timesheets, due times and submission history. Operations can see timesheet content and AI oversight, but not check-in or peer-observation answers or their AI oversight.

Current approval and AI behavior

For morning check-ins, evening check-ins and peer observations, Health approval requires the reviewer to agree or disagree with AI and enter Notes. The note is retained with the review decision. Operations owns timesheet approval; before approving a timesheet, the Operations reviewer records agreement or disagreement with its AI oversight and a reason. Operations can see timesheet oversight, but never health questionnaire or peer-observation answers or their AI reasoning.

AI urgency and AI oversight are separate. Urgency assigns a priority from Critical through Routine. Oversight considers the submission, authorship and subject of peer observations, recent history, timesheets and earlier review context. Wellbeing values are 1–5 ratings, not objective measurements such as hours of sleep. Timesheet context accounts for the recorded work, break, meal and other category totals; it does not describe a recorded break or meal as absent. Peer observations are attributed to the astronaut being described, not mistaken as an observation about the person who submitted it. Oversight is prose rather than bullet points and is assistive context for the authorized reviewer, who makes the decision.

Oversight and mutual accountability

HealthSheets is built so Operations and Health hold each other accountable, without collapsing into a single privileged view of sensitive data.

  • Operations: Sees submission completion status, overdue items, timesheets, timesheet AI oversight, and status-only signals when check-ins or peer observations await Health approval. It does not see their answers, AI oversight, or approval controls. Operations approves timesheets.
  • Health: Sees check-ins, peer observations, timesheets, timesheet completion and pending Operations approval, and AI oversight. Health approves check-ins and peer observations, not timesheets. Health contacts Ops outside the platform when a separate operational action is required.
  • AI (assistive): Provides a third, independent perspective on patterns and priority — not a decision-maker and not a substitute for either department

Operations sees whether a submission is awaiting Health approval, but this status signal does not include Health answers, AI findings or review controls. Separate operational requests based on Health review are handled out of band.

AI role

AI helps Health prioritise asynchronously:

  • Surfaces likely-attention items from questionnaires, peer observations, activity patterns, and trends.
  • Supports triage queues so Health can work through backlog without every signal becoming a push notification.
  • Does not interrupt or reshape the astronaut or Operations notification flow for routine prioritisation (no alert spam from AI ranking).
  • Reasoning and priority for health submissions stay with Health and are not exposed to Operations. Timesheet AI oversight is visible to Operations for its timesheet approval decision; Health can also view that timesheet context.
  • Human review remains authoritative. AI does not approve, close, or escalate operationally on its own.

This oversight model keeps three lanes clear: Operations accountability for mission process, Health accountability for wellbeing monitoring (aligned with OCHMO-TB-016: nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-016-behavioral-health.pdf intent), and AI as an asynchronous prioritisation aid that does not own the notification channel.

Encryption

Questionnaires, peer observations, and other health-related records are encrypted at rest using normal platform/storage encryption (and encrypted in transit). Locally queued offline submissions are encrypted at rest where the device/platform supports it.

Offline operation and synchronisation

Offline use is treated as a distributed system with an unreliable connection. Three things are preserved independently:

  1. The astronaut’s work — submissions do not disappear or get duplicated
  2. Operational state — submission, review, and approval statuses converge correctly
  3. Audit trail — what happened, when, and which device or person initiated it

Astronaut-facing behaviour

Invisible synchronisation. Astronauts do not see:

  • Previous submissions as the primary workflow
  • A synchronisation queue
  • Manual sync controls
  • Connectivity warnings or retry messages as part of normal completion

Completion on the dashboard means the submission was durably saved locally and accepted by the application. Mission Control marks submitted only when the server has received and committed it. Temporary divergence is intentional.

Background mechanisms

  • Durable local outbox (e.g. IndexedDB): Survives restarts and connection loss
  • Service worker for app shell: Caches static assets; not a substitute for the submission queue
  • Idempotency keys: Prevent duplicate submissions and events on retry
  • Exponential backoff + jitter: Retries transient failures without thundering herds
  • Transactional outbox (server): Events are not lost after DB commit
  • Ordered operations / sequence numbers: Preserve dependencies between queued actions
  • Chunked / streaming + resumable uploads: Handle larger payloads on unreliable links
  • Schema versioning: Queued ops survive app updates
  • Server acknowledgements: Confirm when an operation is safely received
  • Incremental sync / change cursor: Download only needed changes
  • Conflict detection: Prevent silent overwrites
  • Audit timestamps: Distinguish client_created_at, server_received_at, server_processed_at
  • Encryption at rest (where supported): Protects locally queued submissions; server-side health records also encrypted at rest
  • Queue health monitoring: Detects stuck devices/queues without exposing health answers
  • Dead-letter handling: Invalid ops are retained for recovery; never silently discarded

Opportunistic sync runs on connectivity, on launch, and periodically while active. Browser Background Sync may help where available but is not a dependency.


Operation queue shape (illustrative)

{
"operation_id": "uuid",
"idempotency_key": "uuid",
"operation_type": "questionnaire.submit",
"mission_id": "mission-123",
"actor_id": "astronaut-456",
"aggregate_id": "submission-789",
"client_created_at": "2026-11-14T09:30:00Z",
"sequence": 12,
"schema_version": 1,
"payload": {},
"status": "pending"
}

Statuses: pending → sending → acknowledged (or failed). Items are removed from the pending queue only after server acknowledgement. Idempotency uniqueness is enforced at the database level. At-least-once delivery with idempotent processing is preferred.

Retry policy (illustrative)

  • Attempt 1: approximately 1s
  • Attempt 2: approximately 2s
  • Attempt 3: approximately 4s
  • Attempt 4: approximately 8s
  • Attempt 5: approximately 16s
  • Attempt 6: approximately 32s
  • Attempt 7+: Cap at 5 minutes

Jitter is added. Network timeouts and 5xx are retried; Retry-After on rate limits is respected; auth expiry pauses retries; invalid payloads are marked failed for resolution; retries stop when permission is revoked. Failed operations never silently disappear.

Conflict strategy

  • Questionnaire draft: Versioned updates; conflicting versions are preserved
  • Submitted questionnaire: Immutable
  • Submitted timesheet: Immutable; corrections are new revisions
  • Peer observation: Immutable
  • Approval: Server-authoritative, immutable audit event
  • Mission configuration: Server-authoritative
  • User permissions: Server-authoritative

Last-write-wins is not used for submitted health information.

Offline approvals

  • Astronauts may complete and submit their own forms offline; payloads stay queued until sync succeeds.
  • Health and Operations approvals require a live server connection (Keycloak session valid).
  • Permission checks happen again on the server when an operation is processed.
  • Previously submitted health records are not automatically cached on every device.


Records retention

For NASA operational adoption, records governance is guided by the NASA Records Management program (nasa.gov/nasa-records-management), NASA Records Retention Schedules (NRRS 1441.1: nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/NPR_attachments/NRRS_1441.1_03232026.pdf), and the requirements in NPR 1441.1E (nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/displayDir.cfm).

Relevant references (confirm with NASA Records Officer before operational adoption):

  • Space-flight personnel health records — e.g. NRRS 01/126.0.B (permanent; see Schedule 8 context)
  • Astronaut medical records historically treated as permanent under Schedule 8 disposition patterns
  • Time and attendance — e.g. NRRS 03/048.0.A (destroy at three years for covered types); do not assume every mission timesheet falls into that category without mapping

NASA federal records policy applies to NASA records and relevant contractors; a Space Apps prototype is designed to follow the policy, with classifications confirmed if adopted operationally.

Explicitly out of scope (this version)

  • Clinical reviews and clinical records management inside HealthSheets
  • Separate Medical vs Behavioural Health role trees
  • Multi-mission assignment for a single astronaut at one time
  • An operational escalation from Health to Operations that exposes a health concern; status-only pending-approval signals are visible to Operations

Product principles (summary)

  1. Daily questionnaires, not sheets astronauts manage.
  2. Astronauts complete check-in; the system owns delivery and data model complexity.
  3. Ops and Health oversee each other’s process accountability without sharing sensitive health content.
  4. AI is a third oversight lens for Health prioritisation — asynchronous, non-authoritative, notification-safe.
  5. Auth via Keycloak / AppDat; server re-checks permissions on every privileged operation.
  6. No clinical system pretence — flag and hand off (see OCHMO-TB-016: nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-016-behavioral-health.pdf).
  7. Encrypt questionnaires and health records at rest (normal encryption in scope; Dex out of scope).
  8. Local completion ≠ server receipt; preserve both timestamps.
  9. Immutable submitted records; append corrections rather than overwrite.
  10. NASA retention schedules govern disposition.
